title: gRPC, GraphQL and when to choose each
scopeHtml: Scope: gRPC and protobuf internals, GraphQL schema and N+1, comparison with REST, decision guide, load balancing and compatibility.

notes.title: The problem: how do two programs talk?
notes.html:
An API style is a contract for how a client asks and a server answers. REST, gRPC and GraphQL are three different contracts. None is "best"; each fixes a different pain.

  • REST: many URLs, one per resource; JSON; works everywhere including browsers.
  • gRPC: you call functions on a remote server (GetUser(id)); binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2; strongly typed.
  • GraphQL: one URL; the client writes a query describing exactly the fields it wants.

Worked example. A profile screen needs name, avatar, last 3 orders. REST: 2 round trips (say 80 ms each on mobile = 160 ms) and over-fetching of unused fields. GraphQL: 1 round trip with only the needed fields. gRPC: 1 call, but the shape is fixed by the service.

Industry examples. Google invented gRPC (from internal Stubby). Facebook invented GraphQL (2012, open sourced 2015) because the News Feed mobile app was drowning in REST round trips. Stripe and GitHub (REST v3) chose REST for broad public reach; GitHub also offers GraphQL v4.

Everyday analogy. Ordering food: REST is a set menu with separate counters, gRPC is a phone line to the kitchen with a fixed order form, GraphQL is "I will describe exactly what I want on my plate".

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "GraphQL replaces REST". It does not; they solve different problems.
  • Not asking who the clients are (public browsers vs internal services) before choosing.

notes.title: gRPC internals
notes.html:
gRPC = Protocol Buffers (a compact binary format) + HTTP/2 + generated client/server code.

You write a .proto file; a compiler generates Kotlin/Java/Go/etc. stubs.

# user.proto
syntax = "proto3";
service UserService {
  rpc GetUser (GetUserRequest) returns (User);
  rpc ListOrders (ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order);   // server streaming
  rpc Chat (stream Msg) returns (stream Msg);                  // bidirectional
}
message GetUserRequest { int64 id = 1; }
message User { int64 id = 1; string name = 2; string email = 3; }

Key facts:

  • Field numbers (= 1) are the identity on the wire, not names. Never reuse or renumber; mark removed ones reserved. That is how backward compatibility works.
  • HTTP/2: multiplexes many calls on one TCP connection, header compression (HPACK), binary framing. No head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer (TCP-level blocking remains).
  • Four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.
  • Deadlines: the client sets a timeout that propagates through the whole call chain; services stop work when it expires. Always set one.
  • Status codes: gRPC has its own (OK, NOT_FOUND, INVALID_ARGUMENT, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, UNAUTHENTICATED, PERMISSION_DENIED...), not HTTP codes.
  • Size: protobuf is typically 3 to 10x smaller than the equivalent JSON and faster to parse (varint encoding: small numbers take 1 byte).
  • Metadata (headers) carries auth tokens and trace ids; interceptors handle logging, auth, retries.

Worked example. JSON user {"id":123456,"name":"Asha","email":"a@x.com"} is about 50 bytes. Protobuf: id as varint (3 bytes + 1 tag), name (1 + 1 + 4), email (1 + 1 + 8), about 20 bytes. At 50,000 calls/s between internal services that saves roughly 1.5 MB/s plus CPU on parsing.

Industry examples. Google (everything internal), Netflix (moved many inter-service calls to gRPC), Square, Uber, Dropbox (gRPC replaced custom RPC), etcd and Kubernetes components (kube-apiserver to etcd), Envoy xDS.

Everyday analogy. A typed form with numbered boxes: both sides agree box 1 is the id, so nobody needs to write the word "id" each time.

Common interview traps.

  • Reusing a protobuf field number with a different meaning (silent data corruption).
  • No deadlines: one slow dependency piles up threads everywhere.
  • Browsers cannot speak native gRPC (no control of HTTP/2 framing); use gRPC-Web with a proxy (Envoy).

notes.title: gRPC in production: load balancing and compatibility
notes.html:
Because gRPC keeps one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, a plain L4 load balancer sends all of a client's calls to one backend. This is the classic gRPC incident: one pod at 95% CPU, others idle after scaling out.

Fixes:

  • L7 balancer that understands HTTP/2 streams (Envoy, Linkerd, Istio, NGINX with grpc_pass, AWS ALB gRPC).
  • Client-side load balancing: client gets all backend addresses (DNS or xDS) and round-robins per call (round_robin policy).
  • Max connection age on servers (for example 5 min with grace) so connections rotate and new pods get traffic.

Compatibility rules for protobuf evolution:

  • Adding a field: safe (old readers ignore it).
  • Removing a field: reserve its number and name.
  • Changing a type: mostly breaking (int32 to int64 is wire-compatible, int to string is not).
  • New enum values: old clients see them as the default/unknown; always handle UNRECOGNIZED.
# Try a gRPC service from the terminal
grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"id": 7}' localhost:9090 UserService/GetUser

Retries: gRPC supports a retry policy via service config (for example 3 attempts, backoff 0.1 s to 1 s, on UNAVAILABLE). Retry only idempotent methods.

Industry examples. Kubernetes + Istio users hit this exact imbalance after enabling gRPC; Lyft built Envoy largely for this kind of L7 balancing.

Everyday analogy. A taxi dispatcher who sends every call from one company to the same driver because "they already have a ride in progress".

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service balances gRPC well (it balances connections, not calls).
  • Retrying non-idempotent RPCs automatically.

notes.title: GraphQL internals
notes.html:
GraphQL is a query language plus a typed schema; the client asks for exactly the fields it needs from a single endpoint (usually POST /graphql).

Schema (the contract):

type User { id: ID!  name: String!  orders(first: Int): [Order!]! }
type Order { id: ID!  total: Int!  items: [Item!]! }
type Query { user(id: ID!): User }
type Mutation { cancelOrder(id: ID!): Order }
type Subscription { orderUpdated(id: ID!): Order }

(! means non-null.)

Query:

query {
  user(id: "7") { name  orders(first: 3) { id total } }
}

Response mirrors the query shape exactly, so no over-fetching and no under-fetching.

How the server runs it: each field has a resolver function. The engine walks the query tree calling resolvers. Three operation types: query (read), mutation (write, run serially), subscription (push over WebSocket/SSE).

The N+1 problem. Query 50 users, each with orders: 1 query for users + 50 queries for orders = 51 DB calls. Fix with DataLoader (batching): collect all 50 user ids in one tick, run one WHERE user_id IN (...). Result: 2 queries.

Other real issues:

  • Query cost / depth attacks: a client can ask user { friends { friends { friends ... } } }. Defend with max depth (for example 8), query cost scoring, timeouts, and persisted queries (allow-list of hashes).
  • Caching: everything is POST to one URL, so HTTP/CDN caching is lost; use persisted queries via GET, response caching per field, or Apollo client normalized cache.
  • Errors: HTTP 200 with an errors array is normal, so monitoring must look inside the body.
  • File upload, rate limiting by cost are extra work.

Worked example. Mobile home screen via REST: /me, /feed, /notifications, /ads = 4 calls, 30 KB. GraphQL: 1 call, 9 KB selecting only displayed fields. On 150 ms RTT networks that is roughly 450 ms saved.

Industry examples. Facebook (origin), GitHub v4 API, Shopify Storefront API, Netflix (federated GraphQL gateway over microservices), Airbnb and Apollo Federation (a gateway stitching many teams' subgraphs).

Everyday analogy. A buffet where you tell the server exactly which items and how much; no pre-packed meal with stuff you throw away.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring N+1 (it is the first follow-up question).
  • Forgetting authorization must be on each resolver/field, not just the endpoint.
  • Exposing introspection and unlimited depth on a public production API.

notes.title: Head-to-head comparison
notes.html:
REST gRPC GraphQL
Transport HTTP/1.1 or 2 HTTP/2 HTTP (usually POST)
Format JSON (text) Protobuf (binary) JSON
Contract OpenAPI (optional) .proto (mandatory) Schema (mandatory)
Typing Weak unless OpenAPI Strong, generated Strong, introspectable
Streaming SSE/WebSocket add-ons Native, 4 modes Subscriptions
Browser support Native Needs gRPC-Web Native
HTTP caching Excellent Poor Poor (needs work)
Payload size Medium Smallest Exactly what you ask
Over/under fetching Common Fixed by RPC shape Solved
Learning curve Lowest Medium Medium to high
Debugging curl, browser grpcurl, needs tooling GraphiQL, needs tooling
Versioning URL/headers Add fields, reserve Deprecate fields

Performance rule of thumb: gRPC is often 2 to 7x faster than REST/JSON for small messages internally, mostly from serialization and connection reuse. Confirm with your own benchmark; numbers vary.

Industry examples. This exact layout (public REST or GraphQL at the edge, gRPC inside) is common at Netflix, Uber and Square.

Everyday analogy. Letters (REST: readable by anyone), a private radio code (gRPC: compact and fast but both sides need the codebook), a custom order form (GraphQL).

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one style for everything. Mixing by layer is normal.
  • Quoting benchmark numbers as facts without caveats.

notes.title: When to choose which
notes.html:
Decision gravity. The API style is a one-way door for external clients (they cannot easily migrate) and a two-way door for internal ones (you control both ends).

Choose REST when:

  • Public or partner API; broad tooling; browsers and curl must work.
  • Resources map cleanly to nouns; caching (CDN, ETag) matters.
  • Team is small, you want the least surprise.

Choose gRPC when:

  • Internal service-to-service, polyglot (Java, Go, Python), high QPS, low latency.
  • You need streaming (telemetry, chat, large downloads in chunks).
  • You want generated clients and enforced contracts in CI.
  • Mobile apps can use gRPC too (battery and bandwidth savings), at the cost of proxy and debugging complexity.

Choose GraphQL when:

  • Many different clients (iOS, Android, web, TV) need different shapes of the same data.
  • Mobile on poor networks where round trips hurt.
  • Many backend services aggregated by one gateway (BFF).
  • You accept the cost: N+1 control, cost limiting, harder caching.

Alternatives and when each breaks:

  • REST breaks when screens need 5+ calls or APIs sprout ?include=, ?fields= hacks. Fix: BFF or GraphQL.
  • gRPC breaks for public web clients and when ops teams lack HTTP/2-aware proxies.
  • GraphQL breaks when the API is simple CRUD (you pay complexity for nothing) or traffic is heavily cacheable.

Worked example. Ride-hailing: driver location updates at 1 per 4 s from 500,000 drivers = 125,000 updates/s. A bidirectional gRPC stream per driver (small protobuf, about 30 bytes of payload) is far cheaper than 125,000 REST POSTs/s each with 500+ bytes of headers. Rider-facing "trip history" is REST or GraphQL.

Industry examples. Uber internal services use gRPC/Thrift-style RPC. Shopify exposes both REST and GraphQL and pushes new features GraphQL-first. Twitter's internal Finagle/Thrift similarly.

Everyday analogy. Choosing between a bus (REST, goes anywhere, everyone can board), a private metro line (gRPC, fast but fixed stations), and a taxi you instruct stop by stop (GraphQL).

Common interview traps.

  • Not stating the client mix and QPS before recommending.
  • Forgetting migration: you can front an existing REST service with a GraphQL gateway without rewriting it.
  • Treating "newer" as "better".

notes.title: Other options worth knowing
notes.html:
• Thrift (Facebook/Apache): like gRPC, older, own transport options.
  • tRPC / JSON-RPC: typed RPC over HTTP+JSON; fine for TypeScript monorepos.
  • WebSockets / SSE: for pushing data, not a request/response style (see the real-time note).
  • OpenAPI (Swagger): describes REST APIs so you can generate clients (Retrofit interfaces) and docs. Gives REST some of gRPC's contract benefits.
  • Webhooks: the server calls your URL when something happens; used by Stripe, GitHub.
  • Kafka/queues: asynchronous messaging when you do not need an immediate reply.

Everyday analogy. Phone call (sync RPC) vs sending a letter (queue): choose by whether you must wait for the answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Using synchronous calls for everything, then suffering cascading failures when one service is slow.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• REST: resource URLs plus JSON, universal and cacheable; best for public APIs.
  • gRPC: protobuf over HTTP/2, typed, streaming, fast; best for internal service-to-service. Never reuse field numbers, always set deadlines, balance per call (L7 or client-side).
  • GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields; fixes over/under-fetching for diverse clients. Watch N+1 (DataLoader), query depth/cost, caching, per-field authorization.
  • Common production layout: GraphQL or REST at the edge, gRPC inside.
  • Choose based on clients, QPS, streaming needs, team skills and caching; edge APIs are one-way doors, internal ones are not.
  • Know the failure modes: gRPC imbalance behind L4, GraphQL N+1 and depth attacks, REST chatty round trips.

questions.promptHtml: What is gRPC and how does it differ from a REST/JSON API?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand the building blocks (protobuf, HTTP/2, codegen) and not just the buzzword.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: gRPC is Protocol Buffers plus HTTP/2 plus generated client and server stubs. I write a .proto contract, generate code, and call remote functions like GetUser(id). Compared with REST/JSON it is binary and smaller, strongly typed, multiplexes calls on one connection and supports four streaming modes. The cost is browser support (needs gRPC-Web) and harder debugging.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
service UserService {
  rpc GetUser (GetUserRequest) returns (User);            // unary
  rpc ListOrders (ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order); // server streaming
  rpc Chat (stream Msg) returns (stream Msg);             // bidirectional
}
message User { int64 id = 1; string name = 2; string email = 3; }

Field numbers identify data on the wire, not names. Varint encoding makes small numbers 1 byte, so protobuf is typically 3 to 10x smaller than JSON. HTTP/2 multiplexes concurrent calls as streams on one TCP connection with HPACK header compression. Deadlines propagate down the call chain. Errors use gRPC status codes (NOT_FOUND, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED), not HTTP codes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"id": 7}' localhost:9090 UserService/GetUser

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking gRPC removes TCP head-of-line blocking (only at the HTTP layer).
  • No deadline set on calls.
  • Calling gRPC directly from a browser.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Four call types? -> Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional.
  2. Why does it need a proxy for browsers? -> Browsers do not expose HTTP/2 framing; gRPC-Web with Envoy bridges it.
  3. How big is the speed gain? -> Often 2 to 7x on small internal messages; verify with your own benchmark.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "faster, binary". Senior explains field-number identity, multiplexing, deadlines and where gRPC does not fit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Internal calls moved to gRPC cut CPU spent on JSON parsing at 50K calls/s.

questions.promptHtml: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do you solve it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first follow-up for any GraphQL claim; it shows whether you understand resolver execution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: GraphQL runs a resolver per field. If I query 50 users and each has orders, the orders resolver runs 50 times, so 1 + 50 = 51 DB queries. The fix is batching with a DataLoader: collect all user ids during one tick, run one WHERE user_id IN (...), then give each parent its slice. That gives 2 queries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
query { users(first: 50) { name orders { id total } } }

Without batching: SELECT users...   + 50 x SELECT orders WHERE user_id = ?
With DataLoader:  SELECT users...   + SELECT orders WHERE user_id IN (50 ids)

The loader also caches per request so the same key is fetched once. Related issues: depth and cost attacks (friends { friends { ... } }), loss of HTTP/CDN caching since everything is a POST to one URL, 200 responses carrying an errors array, and per-field authorization.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
// DataLoader: batch function receives all keys of one tick
DataLoader<Long, List<Order>> loader = DataLoaderFactory.newMappedDataLoader(
    userIds -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderRepo.findByUserIds(userIds)));
val loader = DataLoaderFactory.newMappedDataLoader<Long, List<Order>> { userIds ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { orderRepo.findByUserIds(userIds) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating the DataLoader once globally instead of per request (cross-user cache leak).
  • Ignoring N+1 until production.
  • Authorization only at the endpoint, not per field.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a join solve it? -> Sometimes, but resolvers are independent; batching is the general fix.
  2. How do you stop deep queries? -> Max depth, cost scoring, timeouts, persisted queries.
  3. Why is caching harder? -> POST to one URL; use persisted queries over GET or field-level caching.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines N+1. Senior shows the batch mechanism, per-request scope and the abuse controls around it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mobile home query went from 400 DB calls to 6 after loaders, dropping p99 from 2 s to 300 ms.

questions.promptHtml: Which protobuf changes are backward compatible and which break old clients? Why are field numbers special?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Contract evolution is the heart of running many services; mistakes cause silent corruption.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The wire format identifies fields by number. Adding a field is safe, old readers ignore it. Removing a field is safe if I reserved its number and name so nobody reuses it. Reusing a number with a different meaning silently corrupts data. Changing types is mostly breaking: int32 to int64 is wire-compatible, int to string is not. New enum values show up as unknown/default to old clients.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Safe:      add field, add rpc, add enum value (clients handle UNRECOGNIZED)
Careful:   int32 <-> int64 wire compatible; check semantics
Breaking:  reuse a field number, change int to string, change meaning/unit
Removed:   reserved 4; reserved "legacy_flag";

Because unknown fields are preserved or skipped, old and new binaries can talk during a rolling deploy. Deploy order for additions: server first for new response fields; for new request fields clients may send before servers understand them, since unknown fields are ignored (but the feature will not work until the server upgrades).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reusing a deleted field number.
  • Assuming an unset int equals "absent" (proto3 default is 0).
  • Exhaustive when/switch on enums crashing on new values.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you tell "missing" from 0? -> optional keyword or wrapper types.
  2. How to catch breaks in CI? -> buf breaking against the main branch.
  3. Rolling deploy order? -> Add on the receiving side first, then start sending.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "add fields". Senior covers reserved, enum handling, defaults and automated breaking-change checks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reused field number made an amount field decode as a different value for a day before anyone noticed.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders service moved from REST to gRPC on Kubernetes, behind a ClusterIP Service. Traffic doubled so you scaled from 4 to 12 pods. Ten minutes later:

pod orders-0  cpu 94%   rps 5,100
pod orders-1  cpu 91%   rps 4,900
pod orders-2..11  cpu 3%  rps ~0   (new pods)
latency p99: 1.8s (was 120 ms) ; GC pauses normal ; DB healthy

The client is a long-lived Java service with 2 channels.
questions.promptHtml: Why did scale-out not help, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase pod CPU limits" or "the new pods are broken". The pods are fine; the connections are pinned.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many client instances and channels? Is there a mesh or L7 proxy? What is max connection age? Is the DNS resolver caching?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart or roll the clients to reconnect (they spread over all pods), or temporarily route through an L7 proxy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: gRPC uses one long-lived HTTP/2 connection; ClusterIP balances connections, not calls. Second, client DNS returns only the ClusterIP so it never sees pod addresses. Third, red herring: GC, DB and CPU limits show nothing unusual.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -tn counts per pod, per-pod rps, Envoy or client logs showing a single subchannel.
  5. Root cause: L4 balancing with multiplexed long connections pins all calls from a client to a few pods.
  6. Fix: Short term: server MaxConnectionAge (for example 5 min plus grace) so connections rotate. Long term: L7 balancing via Envoy/Linkerd/Istio or ALB with gRPC, or client-side round_robin using a headless Service and DNS/xDS.
  7. Prevention: Per-pod rps dashboard, load-test after scaling, scale-out acceptance test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Max-connection-age causes reconnect churn (use jitter); a proxy adds a hop and an operational dependency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Streaming calls last for hours -> Age-based rotation does not rebalance them; balance at stream creation and limit stream lifetime.
  • Retries during rotation? -> Only for idempotent methods.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled pods during a sale and the new capacity stayed idle for an hour because every client held an old connection.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises limits.
  • Hire: L4 vs per-call balancing, L7 or client-side fix.
  • Strong hire: includes connection age with jitter, headless Service, streams caveat and a test.

questions.contextHtml:
A mobile team ships a feed screen via GraphQL. After launch DB CPU is 80%. Resolver and query log:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@SchemaMapping(typeName = "Post", field = "author")
public User author(Post p) {
    return userRepo.findById(p.authorId()).orElse(null);   // runs per post
}
@SchemaMapping(typeName = "Post", field = "author")
fun author(p: Post): User? = userRepo.findById(p.authorId).orElse(null)
query { feed(first: 50) { id text author { name avatar } } }
SQL log for one request: 1 x SELECT posts ... ; 50 x SELECT users WHERE id = ?
requests: 2,000/s  -> ~102,000 SQL/s
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and what is your fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a cache" or "add an index". The index is not the problem; the query count is.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the user table index-backed? Are many posts by the same author? Is authorization per field in play?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower the max first from 50 to 20 temporarily; cache author lookups in a short TTL map.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N+1 from the per-parent resolver. Missing index (red herring: lookups are by primary key). Connection pool contention as a side effect.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count SQL statements per request in logs, pg_stat_statements top query by calls, trace span count.
  5. Root cause: One resolver call per post, each running its own query.
  6. Fix: Batch with a request-scoped DataLoader keyed by author id: 1 query for posts + 1 WHERE id IN (...) = 2 queries per request, about 4,000 SQL/s instead of 102,000. Spring for GraphQL offers @BatchMapping to the same effect.
  7. Prevention: Test asserting max SQL count per query, per-request query counter in tracing, N+1 detection in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A cross-request cache hides the problem and can leak per-user data; I would not scope the loader globally.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Author has per-viewer visibility rules -> Authorization inside the batch function, keyed by viewer.
  • Large batch size? -> Chunk the IN list.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single GraphQL field added by a front-end team multiplied database calls by 50 overnight; nobody on the backend had reviewed the query.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds index/cache only.
  • Hire: DataLoader batching.
  • Strong hire: also numbers, per-request scoping, SQL-count test and authz in batch.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing app has 500,000 online drivers sending location every 4 s: 125,000 updates/s. Riders, an admin web console and 12 internal microservices consume these. A teammate proposes plain POST /locations with JSON for everything.
questions.promptHtml: What API style do you pick for each leg and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "REST everywhere for consistency" with no numbers, ignoring per-call overhead.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Update size? Acceptable latency? Must the phone work on bad networks and background? Who are the clients per leg?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable (design); I would start with the highest-volume leg.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Driver app to backend is the hot path: bidirectional or client streaming gRPC with a 30-byte protobuf, one connection per driver. Internal services use gRPC for generated typed clients and deadlines. Admin console and public partners use REST/JSON for browser support and CDN caching. A GraphQL BFF is justified only if rider screens need many different shapes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype a load test: 125K REST POSTs/s means 125K requests with full headers and JSON parse each; compare bytes and CPU against a stream.
  5. Root cause of the choice: Per-request overhead dominates at this rate; streaming amortises connection and header cost.
  6. Fix (the design): gRPC streams from drivers via an L7 proxy, queue (Kafka) behind it, REST for partners and admin.
  7. Prevention: Contract in .proto checked by buf breaking.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: gRPC on mobile adds proxy/debug cost and battery behaviour to test; fallback to REST if carriers or corporate proxies block HTTP/2. One style for everything is not a goal; this is a one-way door externally, two-way internally.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Browser dashboard wants live locations -> Server-sent events or WebSocket fan-out, not gRPC from the browser.
  • 10x drivers -> Shard stream terminators by region/driver id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team unified on one JSON API and spent months on connection and parsing cost; a streaming ingestion path cut fleet cost by a third.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one style, no reasons.
  • Hire: gRPC internal/streaming, REST public.
  • Strong hire: numbers, fallback for mobile networks, layered design and gravity of the choice.

questions.promptHtml: Compare REST, gRPC and GraphQL across caching, typing, streaming, browser support and versioning. How do they coexist in one system?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors choose by constraints and mix styles by layer; juniors pick a favourite.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: REST: HTTP/JSON, universal, best HTTP caching, weak typing unless OpenAPI. gRPC: protobuf over HTTP/2, strict contract, native streaming, smallest payload, needs gRPC-Web for browsers, poor HTTP caching. GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields, fixes over/under-fetching, weak HTTP caching, needs N+1 and cost control. A typical layout is REST or GraphQL at the edge and gRPC between services.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
REST          gRPC            GraphQL
Format       JSON          Protobuf        JSON
Contract     OpenAPI(opt)  .proto (must)   Schema (must)
Streaming    SSE/WS        native, 4 modes Subscriptions
HTTP cache   excellent     poor            poor
Browser      native        gRPC-Web        native
Versioning   URL/headers   add+reserve     deprecate fields
Mobile -> GraphQL BFF -> gRPC Orders / gRPC Users
Partner -> REST public API -> gRPC Orders

Speed numbers (gRPC 2 to 7x on small messages) depend on your payloads; benchmark before quoting.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "GraphQL replaces REST".
  • Quoting benchmarks as facts.
  • Picking one style for every layer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which for a public partner API? -> REST with OpenAPI.
  2. Where does a BFF fit? -> Aggregates many gRPC/REST backends into client-shaped responses.
  3. Can you add GraphQL without rewriting services? -> Yes, a gateway in front of existing REST/gRPC services.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists pros and cons. Senior asks who the clients are, the QPS and cacheability, and says which door is one-way.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A GraphQL gateway over legacy REST cut mobile calls per screen from 5 to 1 without touching the services.

questions.contextHtml:
During a refactor an engineer edits payment.proto. Order-service is still on the old build for another 3 hours (rolling deploy).

// before
message Payment {
  int64  id       = 1;
  int64  amount   = 2;     // paise
  string upi_ref  = 3;
  bool   refunded = 4;
}
// after
message Payment {
  int64  id       = 1;
  string amount   = 2;     // now "19.99"
  string upi_ref  = 3;
  string refund_state = 4; // "NONE" | "FULL"
}
payment-service (new) -> order-service (old):
  warning: unknown/invalid wire type for field 2, order totals = 0
  refunds show as "true" for 40% of orders
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and what is the safe way to make this change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Deploy order-service first." Rollout order cannot fix an incompatible wire change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are payments stored with these types? Any other consumers (analytics, mobile)? Can we roll back right now?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back payment-service; check for corrupted writes and quarantine them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Field 2 changed from varint int64 to length-delimited string: old reader fails to parse. Field 4 reused with a different type, so old readers misinterpret it. Red herring: network errors; the log is a decode problem.
  4. How I'd verify each: Decode a captured message with protoc --decode_raw, compare descriptors with buf breaking.
  5. Root cause: Wire-incompatible type change and reuse of field number 4 with a different meaning.
  6. Fix: Keep amount = 2 as int64 paise, add string display_amount = 5. Keep refunded = 4, add RefundState refund_state = 6 (an enum with UNSPECIFIED = 0). Later reserved 4; once every reader migrated.
  7. Prevention: buf breaking in CI against main, code review checklist for proto changes, reserved on every removal.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual fields cost a little payload and double writes during migration; I would not reuse number 4 under any circumstances.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data already written by the new version -> Reprocess from the source events; the corrupted rows need a backfill.
  • Why was the bool problem silent? -> Wire type mismatch is dropped or misparsed depending on the runtime; never rely on it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reused field number produced wrong ledger amounts for a few hours; the fix was easy, the reconciliation was not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes rollout order only.
  • Hire: add new numbers, keep old ones.
  • Strong hire: finds both bugs, uses buf breaking, reserved and a data reconciliation plan.

questions.contextHtml:
Public GraphQL API for a social app, 8M DAU. At 02:10 DB CPU hits 100% and p99 goes from 200 ms to 25 s. Gateway shows only 900 rps (normal 1,500). Slow-query log and the offending query:

query { user(id:"1") { friends(first:100) { friends(first:100) { friends(first:100)
  { friends(first:100) { name posts(first:100) { comments(first:100) { text }}}}}}}}

rows touched: ~10^8 per query ; 6 clients using it ; all HTTP 200
WAF: no alerts (valid JSON, POST /graphql)
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate now, find the root cause and design the defences.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rate limit by requests per second." Request count is low; each request is enormously expensive.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is introspection open? Are these clients authenticated? Can we identify the queries by hash? Is there a query timeout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the offending clients/IPs, set a hard execution timeout, reduce DB statement timeout, and reject queries above depth 6 at the gateway.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unbounded query depth and list sizes; deliberate abuse or a buggy client; missing batching making each level N+1. Red herring: traffic was lower than normal, so not volumetric.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log operation hash with duration and DB time, group by client, compute the estimated cost of the query.
  5. Root cause: Cost is determined by the client's query and nothing bounded it.
  6. Fix: Max depth (for example 8), complexity scoring with a per-request budget and a per-client cost-per-minute rate limit (not requests per second), pagination limits (first <= 50), timeouts, persisted queries (allow-list of hashes) for first-party clients, introspection off on public prod, DataLoader everywhere.
  7. Prevention: Metric of cost per operation, alert on top operations by DB time, load tests with adversarial queries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Persisted-only mode blocks third-party developers; I would not disable GraphQL as a whole, and I would not rely on the WAF for application-level cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner needs ad hoc queries -> Higher budget under a separate key with quotas.
  • How do you monitor with all-200 responses? -> Record errors inside the body and per-operation latency metrics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One nested query from a misconfigured client drove a database to its limit while the rps graph looked calm.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: request-rate limit.
  • Hire: depth and timeout limits.
  • Strong hire: cost-based limiting, persisted queries, observability by operation and incident handling.

questions.contextHtml: A new CTO says: "Our Android app makes five REST calls to render the home screen and it is slow. Let us move everything to GraphQL." You have 18 engineers, a REST API with 90 endpoints used by Android, iOS, web and 30 partners, 3M DAU, mostly 4G, median RTT 150 ms. Home screen calls: /me, /feed, /notifications, /ads, /config.
questions.promptHtml: What do you say and what do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, GraphQL is the modern standard." No data, no migration thinking, treats it as reversible.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly is slow: round trips, payload size, or one slow backend call? Are the calls sequential or parallel? How many screens have this issue? Is caching important? Who maintains the schema?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Parallelise the five calls and enable compression; measure. Five sequential calls at 150 ms RTT cost 750 ms, parallel about 150 ms plus the slowest.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Calls are sequential or blocked on a slow endpoint. Over-fetched payloads (30 KB where 9 KB is used). Only the home screen is painful, not the whole API. Red herring: the protocol is rarely the bottleneck.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace the app startup, check per-endpoint p95, and look at bytes per call.
  5. Root cause: Probably chattiness on one screen plus no aggregation.
  6. Fix: Add a single GET /home aggregate endpoint (a BFF) that fans out to the services in parallel and returns only needed fields; GraphQL is justified later if many screens and clients need flexible shapes.
  7. Prevention: Performance budget per screen, tracing in the app.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A full migration costs N+1 control, query-cost limits, caching work and team training, with a one-way door for external consumers; I would pilot GraphQL as a gateway over the existing REST on one client before committing. REST stays for partners.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• iOS, TV, web all need different fields -> Strong argument for a GraphQL BFF.
  • Offline support? -> Normalised client cache helps; evaluate Apollo cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team rewrote to GraphQL for a latency problem that turned out to be one slow ads call; a BFF endpoint and a timeout fixed it in a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees without data.
  • Hire: asks what is slow and proposes BFF.
  • Strong hire: quantifies, pilots GraphQL as a gateway, keeps REST for partners and states reversibility.

questions.contextHtml:
You are moving the checkout path (Gateway -> Cart -> Pricing -> Inventory) from REST to gRPC, one hop at a time, at 8,000 rps. Early canary at Cart -> Pricing shows:

Gateway timeout 3s ; Cart client no deadline ; Pricing -> Inventory deadline 10s
Inventory p99 6s during a cache flush
threads in Cart: 200/200 busy, queue growing ; Gateway 504 rate 18%
retry policy: 3 attempts on UNAVAILABLE and DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, incl. ReserveStock
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the setup and how do you make the migration safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the thread pool." More threads wait longer on a slow dependency; cascading failure grows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which RPCs are idempotent? Is the gateway deadline propagated? What is the error budget? Can we dual-run REST and gRPC per hop?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shift the canary back to REST via a flag; reduce retries to zero for non-idempotent calls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Deadlines are not propagated (the gateway gives up at 3 s while downstream keeps working to 10 s). Retrying DEADLINE_EXCEEDED on a slow service multiplies load (retry storm). Retrying ReserveStock may double-reserve. Threads are held by slow calls.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace spans showing remaining deadline per hop, retry counters, duplicate reservation count in Inventory.
  5. Root cause: No end-to-end deadline budget, and retries applied to non-idempotent methods and to deadline errors.
  6. Fix: Propagate one deadline from the gateway (3 s) and let each hop use what remains (Cart 2.5 s, Pricing 1.5 s, Inventory 800 ms); retry only idempotent calls and only on UNAVAILABLE, max 2 attempts with backoff and jitter and a retry budget; an idempotency key for ReserveStock; bulkhead/limit concurrent calls to Inventory with a circuit breaker.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test with slow Inventory, dashboard of DEADLINE_EXCEEDED per hop, per-method retry config reviewed in PRs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual-running both protocols doubles ops for a while but gives instant rollback; I would not migrate all hops at once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Streaming RPC deadline? -> Deadline covers the whole stream; use keepalive and per-message timeouts.
  • Hedged requests? -> Only for idempotent reads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration canary tripled load on a recovering service because both the client library and the mesh were retrying the same failures.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases threads/timeouts.
  • Hire: deadline propagation and retry only idempotent calls.
  • Strong hire: retry budgets, idempotency key, circuit breaker, per-hop canary and rollback.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review of a Saturday outage of a product-search feature served by GraphQL at 20K rps. Findings:

- Uptime check: HTTP 200 for the entire 4h incident
- Body: {"data":{"search":null},"errors":[{"message":"upstream timeout"}]}  -> 31% of requests
- CDN hit ratio fell from 78% (old REST /search?q=) to 4% after the GraphQL move
- Origin egress cost +3.1x; p50 latency +90 ms
- Alert fired only after customers tweeted, 52 minutes in
questions.promptHtml: What failed in the platform choices and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "GraphQL was a mistake." Overreaction; the issues are monitoring and caching design, both fixable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are searches personalised? How many distinct queries make up the top 90% of traffic? Which clients need dynamic shapes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the search incident: serve stale cache and degrade gracefully; add a synthetic probe that checks the body.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Monitoring counted HTTP status only, so partial failure was invisible. Everything is POST to one URL, so the CDN cannot cache. A small set of queries accounts for most traffic.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute the error share in bodies, the number of distinct operation hashes vs traffic, the cacheability of the responses.
  5. Root cause: We adopted GraphQL without adapting observability, and gave up HTTP caching without a replacement.
  6. Fix: Instrument per-operation success and latency from the errors array (use a name per operation); set SLOs on that; persisted queries over GET with Cache-Control so the CDN works for public queries; response caching per field; return a non-200 status for total failure where the server can; alert on body errors.
  7. Prevention: Operation-level dashboards, runbooks and a launch checklist covering caching, cost limiting, errors and monitoring for any new API style.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: For a highly cacheable, simple read like search, keep REST (or both): GraphQL adds cost where the shape does not vary. I would not turn off the errors array semantics, but would make partial failures measurable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Personalised results -> Cache only the non-personalised part, use a key with segment.
  • Partial data policy? -> Define which fields are critical and fail the whole response for them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard stayed green during an hours-long GraphQL partial failure because it watched only HTTP status codes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the technology.
  • Hire: monitors bodies, adds caching via persisted GET.
  • Strong hire: ties choice to workload, operation SLOs, launch checklist and says REST remains right for search.
